Texas House, Phase Two
Texas House · working brief · Sept 2026 · confidential

Texas House,
Phase Two

Texas House started as an event. It is becoming a company, and the brand is ascending: the name now carries more than the weekends that made it. Phase Two is the work of building the company that can carry the brand. Everything in motion right now is one of three jobs: Part I builds the board that raises the money and holds us to the standard. Part II settles what we sell, who buys it, and what they get. Part III looks past the activations at the lines of business they could become. The first two meet in the middle — the board brief answers the positioning session's first question.

Oct 2026 · Race Weekend, Austin  ·  Jan 2027 · DC Welcome, Capitol Hill  ·  Mar 2027 · SXSW, the flagship

How to review this

This is a working document, read by the team and by the people we are talking to. Whoever you are, your notes are welcome: go section by section, and say the thing you would say out loud. There are two ways to leave feedback, depending on how you opened this.

If Will added you by email, select any text in the section you are responding to and choose Comment. The comment stays pinned to that passage and everyone can see it and reply.

If you opened the public link, comments are switched off by the platform. Use the add feedback link at the top of any section, or the Feedback button at the bottom right. Pick the section, pick a kind, write your notes with bullets if you like, and add as many as you want. When you are done, press Copy batch and paste it into an email to will@texashouse.org. Your notes wait in this browser between visits, so you can read in sittings and send one batch at the end.

One point per note works best. Everything is collected by section for the next pass.

Part I: Who governs it

Prepared for Christin Evans. A board that can do three things: help us raise money, hold us to a standard, and bring in the people and partners we need to grow.

"Christin, you told me a board is for governance and recruitment. I agree. Read this as a starting point — I want your judgment on all of it. What I am asking of you: sit on the board as a director, chair the governance and nominating committee, and help me finish the slate and set up the process that keeps the board honest and productive year after year." — Will

§01

What the board exists to produce

add feedback

The board of a private, for-profit corporation. Directors owe their duty to the shareholders, hold equity, and are elected each year by the controlling shareholder. Board members serve three main functions:

JobWhat it means
RaiseBring in sponsors, partners, and capital. Every seat maps to a source of money, or a source of legitimacy that leads to money.
GovernHold the company to a standard. Approve what needs approving. Ask the hard questions before a partner or investor does.
RecruitReach further than the founding team can. Bring in the people who make Texas House bigger than its founder.

Equity is the engine. Directors raise money because they own part of the outcome — the vesting cliff and the annual election tie the reward to the work.

Shareholders
Elect directors annually. Will holds control.
Board of Directors
5 seats · one-year terms · fiduciary, votes
Governance & Nominating Committee
Advisory Board
No vote, no liability.
Network and doors. Forms immediately.
Officers
CEO · Secretary · Treasurer
Appointed by the board; present, don't vote.
Vice presidents are staff roles, not officers.

Five seats — odd number, no ties; the chairman holds the tiebreak until seat five fills. Three independents alongside the founder. Quarterly meetings, written consents between. One committee to start; finance or audit follows when the numbers warrant it.

§04

Terms for directors

add feedback
TermOne year, elected annually by shareholders. Re-election follows the annual review by the governance and nominating committee.
CompensationRestricted common stock at seating. No cash; reasonable expenses reimbursed. Grant size set per seat, informed by the governance chair.
Vesting12-month cliff — nothing vests before the first anniversary; then monthly over 36 months. Leave before the cliff, hold nothing. 83(b) filed within 30 days of grant; the company provides the form and deadline.
ExpectationsFour quarterly meetings, in person where possible. Written consents inside five business days. A written year-one expectation tied to the seat spec. Conflicts disclosed, recusal where appropriate.
ProtectionD&O insurance before the first meeting. Indemnification in the bylaws. A director agreement covering term, grant, expectations, and exit.

Why the cliff instead of a probation period: a grant at seating with a 12-month cliff does the same job and is the structure experienced directors expect. The company should be worth more in a year — waiting to grant makes the stock a larger taxable event. A director with a grant on paper is committed in a way a director with a promise is not.

§06

How seats get filled

add feedback

The board recruits the board, starting with seat five: specification first — candidates are measured against the spec, not against who is available. The committee owns the search. Every seated director puts forward three names from their own network. Warm approach, one conversation with Will, then a written offer — seat, term, grant, vesting, year-one expectation, D&O — before anyone says yes. Committee recommends, board approves, shareholders elect.

What we are not doing: filling a seat to fill it — an open seat with a live search reads as deliberate, a weak director does not. Recruiting from the founder's immediate circle — the people who can raise money for Texas House are mostly people we have not met yet. Promising equity before the spec, the expectation, and the paperwork are set.

Part II: What we sell

This part is not for writing a tagline. It is for agreeing on what we sell, who buys it, and what they get. The tagline falls out of that in about ten minutes once the rest is settled.

Every line we run in market today is about Texas. Not one is about the buyer. A sponsor hears all of them and still has no idea what they are purchasing — which is why every meeting turns into "so how do you make money, and what are we paying for?" That question is not skepticism. It is the buyer trying to do our job for us.

The pitch, at four lengths

add feedback

The tagline — proposed (full hero in §08.5)
Where Texas meets the world.

Four words, bidirectional, implies a place. "Recognizing Texcellence" is already out of the rebuilt hero — it survives as the About-page headline, which is exactly the "campaign line only" fallback. Ten seconds

Texas House is the platform for Texas's global moment. We build the room where Texas business, capital, and culture meet the world, at the moments the world is already watching.

Thirty seconds — money question pre-answered

Texas is having its biggest run since oil, and there is still no front door to it. If you are a country, a company, or a university trying to plug into Texas, there is no obvious room to walk into. We build that room. Three or four times a year, at the moments the world already shows up, Texas House is the Texas platform. We are partner-funded today, the way a sports team is: partnerships first, and tickets as the next line as the events grow. Partners underwrite the programming and the venue, and in exchange they get named placement, a voice in the programming, and direct introductions to the people they came to meet.

Two minutes — partner meeting

The moment. Texas is the eighth largest economy in the world. Since 2020 it has absorbed more corporate relocation, more energy and defense capital, and more cultural weight than any other state. Everyone knows this is happening. Almost nobody outside Texas knows how to get in.

The gap. There is no front door. A British trade delegation, a university commercializing research, a fund looking at Texas deal flow — they all end up cold-emailing the same five people.

What we built. Texas House is that front door. We take the moments when the world is already assembled — SXSW, race weekend, SXSW London — and build the Texas platform inside them. Curated programming by day, culture at night, deliberate introductions throughout.

How it works. Partner-funded, with [N — pending §10] ways in: named placement, programming voice, curated introductions, guest list, year-round content.

The proof. What the site already says with a straight face, from live data: five activations, two cities, 56 programd sessions, 47 partners. Attendance and outcome numbers are the remaining gap — [INSERT before this ships].

What we are building. Every activation adds to the network. The people we convene now run Texas in ten years. Partners in early are in the room permanently.

Part III: Where it could go

Lines of business beyond the activations. Nothing here is decided. First, a foundation that lets partners give as well as buy. Then three reference models with their sources, and two Texas House concepts built from them: a corporate lane that accelerates business the Texas way, and an individual lane that gives operators a room of their own.

§17.5

The Texas House Foundation

add feedback
concept, for discussion

A nonprofit foundation, started by Texas House and run alongside it, for the part of our work that partners want to give to rather than buy. Texas House stays the company that sells the activations. The foundation becomes the place the philanthropy lives, and it opens doors a for-profit company never can.

What it is

The Texas House Foundation would be a Texas nonprofit corporation applying for 501(c)(3) status as a public charity. Texas House would be its founding and operating partner, the role we have been calling the fiduciary partner: Texas House designs and runs the programs the foundation pays for, and is paid for that work at fair market value under a written services agreement.

One precision worth getting right early. The fiduciary duty itself sits with the foundation's own board, and it runs to the foundation, not to Texas House. Texas House is the partner that makes the work happen. The board is what makes the gifts safe.

It stands between Texas House and the partners who want to fund charitable work. A partner can sponsor Texas House, give to the foundation, or both, as two separate relationships paid from two separate budgets.

Two relationships, kept separate
Sponsorship, to Texas HouseGift, to the foundation
What it isA purchase: named placement, a programming voice, introductions (§13)A charitable contribution to a program with a mission
What the partner getsThe partner packageThanks, by name or logo on the program. No advertising, no package
Tax treatmentA business expenseA charitable deduction. If the donor receives something of value, only the part above that value counts
Whose budgetMarketingGiving: corporate responsibility, a company foundation, or personal philanthropy
Where the money goesTexas House revenueThe foundation's programs. Texas House is paid only for work it does, at fair value
What it could do for us
suggested
Budgets

Two budgets at the same partner.

Most companies keep their giving separate from their marketing. Today we can only ask for the marketing budget. With a foundation, one relationship can fund a sponsorship and a program, from two different lines.
Tax

Gifts that count as charity.

A contribution to a 501(c)(3), donated goods and services included, can be deductible; a sponsorship cannot. Employers' matching-gift programs apply too. For the individual operators in lane two (§20), that is often what tips a yes.
Access

Money a company cannot take.

Private foundations, universities and many public bodies fund nonprofits and cannot fund a for-profit company. Grants for culture, education and civic programs come within reach.
Mission

The network, opened up.

Fellowships and scholarships that bring young Texans, artists, filmmakers and founders into the rooms at SXSW, SXSW London and race weekend. The network of ascending leaders, extended to people who could never buy a seat.
Public partners

A clean way in for public partners.

Policy makers, economic developers and consulates often cannot sponsor a company. Supporting a foundation's public program is a door they can walk through in the open.
Board

Seats that do not need equity.

Civic leaders and former officeholders who would never join a company board will join a foundation's. The government door on the seat 7 list (§02) may fit here first.
The rules that keep it clean
  • The money serves the mission, not Texas House. No part of a 501(c)(3)'s earnings may benefit its creator or insiders. Texas House can be paid for real work at fair market value, approved by the board with Texas House people stepping out of that vote.
  • A gift is not a sponsorship. A donor can be thanked by name and logo. The moment they receive the partner package, it is a purchase. When a donor gets something of value for a payment over $75, the foundation has to say so in writing, and only the part above that value is deductible.
  • Thanks, not advertising. A company supporting the foundation can be acknowledged by name and logo. Comparative or qualitative language about its products turns that into advertising, which the foundation would owe tax on.
  • An independent board. Texas House people can sit on it. They should not be the majority.
  • Broad support. To stay a public charity rather than a private foundation, more than a third of its support over five years has to come from the public: many donors, grants, government. A foundation funded by two partners does not pass.
  • Separate everything. Its own bank account, books, minutes and annual return, and a written license to use the Texas House name.
How it could start
  1. Now, without a new entity. Run the first charitable program through a fiscal sponsor. Austin Creative Alliance extends its 501(c)(3) status to arts projects and one-time events, so gifts to a named project are tax-deductible today, for a 10% administrative fee and a $180 annual membership. It fits the cultural programs. It does not fit everything.
  2. In parallel, form the foundation. A Texas nonprofit certificate of formation is a $25 filing with the Secretary of State. Adopt bylaws and a conflict-of-interest policy, seat an independent board, and file IRS Form 1023: a $600 fee, and the IRS currently decides 80% of applications within 191 days.
  3. When the determination letter arrives, move the programs across, sign the services agreement with Texas House, and announce it.
A decision this raises: the name

A Houston nonprofit, The Texas Alcoholism Foundation, Inc., has operated as The Texas House since 1965, running residential addiction treatment. A charity called the Texas House Foundation would sit right beside it in search results, in donor databases, and possibly in a trademark review. It needs a clearance search with counsel before anything is filed.

Also to settle
  • Who chairs the foundation's board, and who else sits on it.
  • The first program it funds.
  • Whether a giving tier belongs in the membership lanes in §20.
  • This does not change §10. Texas House stays a for-profit C-corp; the foundation sits beside it.

A concept for discussion, not legal or tax advice. Counsel and a CPA who work with nonprofits should review the structure before anything is filed. Sources: IRS, Form 1023 fee · IRS, processing times · IRS, inurement and private benefit · IRS, quid pro quo contributions · IRS, sponsorship or advertising · public support test · Texas SOS, Form 202 · Austin Creative Alliance · The Texas House, Houston

§19

The flagship house

add feedback

Two private clubs already prove the physical model in Texas. What they built, what they charge, and what each one says about the room it wants.

They come from opposite directions. Park House is the Texas-born version: founded in Dallas by hoteliers who had lived inside London's clubs, opened in Highland Park Village in 2018, and grown to a second house in Houston. Soho House is the global one: a London chain of forty-eight Houses in nineteen countries whose first Texas house landed on South Congress in 2021. One shows what a club built here can charge; the other shows that the international member will come to Austin for it.

Park House · Dallas and Houston

The London club, translated to Texas.

Opened 2018 in Highland Park Village. Founded by John and Deborah Scott (John ran Rosewood and Belmond) with Megan and Brady Wood (WoodHouse). Modelled on London's private clubs, 5 Hertford Street and Annabel's among them, and positioned as the alternative to the country club and the business club. Three dining rooms, private dining, library and living rooms, a gallery with a rotating art program, screenings, live performance, tastings. Houston opened December 2023: 25,000 square feet at 4411 San Felipe.
The money: Resident members (30+) pay a $7,500 initiation and $292 a month; Junior (23 to 30) $2,800 and $146; non-resident $4,800 and $146. Founding members paid $25,000 with dues waived for life. A capped Culture membership runs $500 a year.

Sources: parkhousedallas.com/membership · PaperCity, 2023

Soho House · Austin

A global brand's first Texas room.

Opened summer 2021 at 1011 South Congress in the Music Lane development, the first House in Texas. Forty-six bedrooms across two floors, a rooftop pool and bar, a screening room, Club Cecconi's, Dante's HiFi bar, a gym partnership. Interiors built with around seventy local artisans and Texas designers, in what the company calls Texas Modernism. Membership is by application: a photo, an occupation, your interests.
The money: Local House membership in Austin is quoted from $937.50 a quarter; press reports put the annual figure between roughly $2,650 and $3,750. Every House, all forty-eight Houses in nineteen countries, is $4,300 a year. Under-27 pricing runs $475 a quarter. Soho Friends, the entry product, is $130 a year.

Sources: sohohouse.com · Austin · membership · Austin American-Statesman, 2021

What the two are worth
Soho House & CoPark House
OwnershipPublic on the NYSE from July 2021 (SHCO). Taken private on 29 January 2026 by a group led by MCR Hotels' Tyler Morse, with Ron Burkle's Yucaipa keeping control and Goldman Sachs Alternatives rolling its stakePrivate. Owned by its four founders through WoodHouse and the Scotts
Valuation$2.7 billion at the take-private, $9.00 a share. Market capitalisation ran about $1.76 billion in its last stretch as a listed companyNo public valuation. About $14 million in outside equity over its life, per CB Insights. It leases its space in Highland Park Village rather than owning it; the money built out and operated the clubs
Revenue$1.20 billion in fiscal 2024, up 7%. Membership fees $418 million of that, up 17%Private. Data-vendor estimates range from about $12 million to $23 million a year across the two houses; treat as a rough order of magnitude
ProfitAdjusted EBITDA $131.9 million in 2024, an 11% margin. Net losses for most of its thirty years; first net profit mid-2025Not disclosed
Scale212,447 members, 45 Houses at end of 2024, 48 todayTwo houses. A waitlist of about 6,500 in Dallas at the Houston announcement. Founding memberships sold at $25,000

Sources: Los Angeles Business Journal, Jan 2026 · Soho House FY2024 results · Macrotrends, SHCO market cap · CB Insights, Park House · PaperCity, 2023

What the numbers say

The buyers paid about 2.2 times revenue and 20 times EBITDA for Soho House, and they paid it for membership fees: the one line that grew 17% while food and rooms stood still. Membership is the asset. Park House shows the other end of the scale: a two-house Texas club is a business in the low tens of millions, built on about $14 million of outside money and a $25,000 founding-member device. That is the size of thing a Texas House flagship would be, and the Soho multiple is what a membership book is worth if it keeps growing.

What the two models have in common, and what we would do differently

Both sell the same thing: a room that is hard to get into, programd so there is a reason to come back, with food and drink carrying the daily economics and initiation fees carrying the capital. Both lead with culture, not business, and let business happen. Both price the individual around three to four thousand dollars a year, plus an entry fee at Park House.

The Texas House difference is the calendar. Neither club has a moment the whole world attends. We do, three or four times a year, and a house is what makes those moments a year-round relationship instead of a week. Park House proves a Texas-founded club can charge London prices; Soho House proves the global buyer will come to South Congress. A Texas House flagship sits between them: the place a delegation lands, a founder brings a counterpart, a partner hosts, on the weeks that matter and every week between.

§20

Two lanes, one ladder

add feedback
concept, for discussion

Built from the three references above and from what we already sell. Names are placeholders.

Lane one · Corporate

Business the Texas way.

A business-development accelerator for corporate partners. Not a sponsorship with a logo on a wall; a year-round program that puts a company in front of the capital, counterparts and customers it came to Texas for. The Boardroom corporate tier is the reference shape; our activations are the delivery mechanism.
What it includes: a co-curated session at one activation a year; a stated number of curated introductions per quarter; delegation hosting when their people are in Texas; a seat at the founder dinners; brand spotlights in the newsroom; first call on programming at the house once it exists.
Who buys: the place-marketers and institutions from Part II, §14: the consulate, the chamber, the exchange, the university. They already fund us by the weekend; this makes it by the year.
Lane two · Individual

A room of their own.

Membership for the operators: founders, investors, oil and energy people, the builders of contemporary Texas. Somewhere to hang out and do business in the same evening, the way Park House members do in Dallas. Programming with a reason, a bar worth staying at, and the network in the room, not on a list.
What it includes: member spaces inside every activation; the dinners and the salons between them; the house, when it exists, as the daily address; tailored introductions on request; guest privileges for the counterpart they bring.
Price anchors: Boardroom $1,800 to $3,600 a year; Soho House Austin roughly $2,650 to $3,750; Park House about $3,500 in dues plus $7,500 to join. Texas House should sit inside that band, with an entry fee only once there is a house to enter.
How it ladders with what exists
RungWhat it isStatus
Activation partnerThe existing tiers, presenting through in-kind, bought by the weekendSells today
Corporate memberLane one: the year-round accelerator, priced above any single activationConcept
Club memberLane two: the individual, priced in the Boardroom to Soho bandConcept; the inquiry form already lists Membership as an interest
Founding member of the houseThe Park House device: a large one-time fee, dues waived for life, capped, closed once the house opens. A capital raise dressed as a membership, which is exactly what the board's raise mandate needsConcept; depends on the flagship
Questions this raises for Part I and Part II
  • The entity question in §10 gets sharper: memberships and a founding-member raise are a for-profit's tools. The board brief already assumes the C-corp; this is why it matters.
  • Two products for one buyer is a pricing problem. A consulate that is a corporate member should not also be sold a presenting partnership at full rate; the ladder needs a rule for that, the same way in-kind needed one in §14.
  • A house is a real-estate and hospitality business before it is a network. It needs an operator in the way Park House has the Scotts and Woods. Seat six or seat seven on the board may be that person.
  • Sequence: lane one can start this season inside the existing activations. Lane two needs the house, or at least the salons, to be real. The founding-member device only works once there is a floor plan to show.
